1 bunch celery (rinsed and cut into chunks--I don't like celery so I leave the pieces big enough to easily pick out, but the flavor is important)

1 onion--chop/mince about half of it.

(The three items above, by the way, are a mirepoix [meer-pwah] and are the basis of a number of soups and stews)

You will also need:

white wine

chicken stock or chicken stock cubes/paste (I use Better than Bouillon)

butter

flour

poultry seasoning or a mix of herbs you like--good ones are Herbs de Provence, basil, marjoram, thyme, oregano...whatever combination you like. A hint of nutmeg is not unwelcome here, either.

You can also add a little lemon juice if you like

And of course chicken. I'm not a fan of dark meat and I usually do a quicker version of this, so I buy a 2-lb or so pkg of chicken tenders (raw chicken, not breaded or anything) because they taste good and cook fast. Sometimes I'll buy a small package of thighs for extra flavor, or bone-in skin-on breasts (the bones and skin add some flavor, but again, it's good without them so it's up to you/how much time you have). Traditionally a whole chicken in used, but the reason I stopped doing that as much is the length of time it takes for a whole chicken to cool and be shredded, plus using the whole chicken sometimes results in bits of skin and bone in the soup that need to be found and picked out. But if you want to use a whole chicken, the soup is the same, you just boil it longer--until the chicken is done--and let it sit half an hour or so to cool before shredding it with your fingers or two forks.

So:

Sweat the mirepoix in a good-sized pot with a lid. "Sweating" means cooking in a little oil with salt & pepper at a very low temp--you should barely hear the sizzle--for a good ten-fifteen minutes until the onions are soft. Once that's done, you have a few options, depending on what chicken you're using:

for a whole chicken or skin-on bone-in pieces, you can scoop the veg out of the pot and turn up the heat a little to brown the chicken (sometimes I skip this, but it does add flavor). Once it's brown (or if you're skipping that step), pour in a good splash of white wine--about half a cup - one cup (you can omit the wine, too, if you happen to be a teenager without access to it) and/or chicken stock--3-4 cups at least, you want enough to cover the chicken pieces by an inch or so (if using a whole chicken, don't cover it, because that's too much liquid; just use enough liquid to almost cover it and make sure to turn it once in a while. The heat from the simmering liquid will cook it all once the lid is on).

If you're using chicken tenders, add the wine and stock and let the veg simmer for 20 min or so before adding the chicken pieces, because the chicken will cook much faster than the carrots/celery. You don't want the veg falling apart necessarily but neither is it nice when it's crunchy (IMO).

At this point, pour out one cup of milk (for the dumplings) and set it aside to warm up a bit. You want it around room temp. You can skip this if you like and use cold milk, but they rise better if the milk has a chance to warm up for even 15 min or so.

So simmer the pot, covered, until the chicken is cooked. Remove big pieces/while chicken and set aside to cool. Taste the liquid for seasonings, add more of whatever you think it needs. (If you use tenders, you can use two forks to shred them right in the pot, or remove them if you prefer. Shred the chicken.

Now. Scoop out some of the cooking liquid into a measuring cup--you want about half a cup of liquid in a one cup measuring cup or larger. Add flour to the liquid until it's like a runny paste. Pour the mix back into the soup and stir--this will thicken the soup a bit.

For the dumplings:

Sift together (You really do need to sift it!) in a large bowl:

2 C flour

3 tsp baking powder (not baking soda, baking powder)

1 tsp salt

Using a pastry cutter or two forks/your hands, cut in 2 Tbsp butter or shortening/lard (butter has best flavor). 2 Tbsp is 30g, if that makes it easier. I usually go a little over and use about 35g. Cut or rub it in until no big chunks remain, you want the butter in tiny flour-covered pieces.

Add about 1/4 C dried parsley to the mixture, and stir it in or use the pastry cutter to mix it in. I usually just grab a good handful of the parsley and crush it in my hand a little as I drop it in. You can use fresh if you want, but you'll need to chop it up and use about half the amount. The dumplings taste good with the dried and the green flecks look pretty, so I don't bother.

Make sure the soup--with chicken added back in--is at a good strong simmer/mild boil now.

Pour the milk into the dimpling mix and stir until it's all mixed--it will be a sticky, lumpy dough. Use a large spoon to drop heaps of dumpling dough onto the soup. Work quickly. The second you drop the last bit of dough onto the soup, cover the pot with the lid, and after a few seconds, turn the heat down to barely a simmer. (I find the Low setting on most stoves is too low, but some are too high, in which case use a diffuser or you'll need to keep moving the pot/removing it from heat for a few seconds to avoid burning the bottom of the soup. You CANNOT OPEN THE POT TO CHECK, unfortunately, because it will make the dumplings hard. The POT MUST STAY COVERED FOR TWENTY MINUTES. I find that if I lean close to the pot at the right temp, I will be able to just barely hear it simmering. This does take a little practice, unfortunately, but it's worth it. You might also have a stove with a perfect Simmer setting, which is awesome.

So after twenty minutes, take the lid off and check. The dumplings should be firm (but not hard); when you poke them with your finger or a fork you should be able to easily see that they have a nice bready sort of texture. If you poke them and they stick to your finger/the fork they're not done enough; cover the pot and give them another minute or two (at this point they have risen enough and are close enough to done that this won't affect the texture).

Let the soup cool a bit. Serve in bowls, with one or two dumplings per person.

Beef Barley soup:

This, like many/most soups, is more a method than a recipe. Almost all the ingredients are optional, so you can make it to your taste, but this is what I generally use:

Minced onion & celery (Mirepoix without carrot, but you can use carrot if you can't find a bag of frozen veg with carrot)

Minced garlic or shallot (half a large shallot, 2-3 garlic cloves) (this is optional)

1-2 lbs stew beef or ground beef

1-2 potatoes, cut in bite-sized pieces

1 bag frozen chopped veg--peas, corn, carrots

1-2 C pearl barley

1 can tomato paste or 1 small can diced tomatoes, or both

good mustard, like a dijon mustard--you'll use a big spoonful of this (optional if you hate mustard or don't have any, but you really don't taste mustard in the soup)

white wine (optional)

Beef stock or Beef Better than Bouiilon--about 3-4 C

Worcestershire Sauce

Bay leaf

Seasonings: thyme, dash of nutmeg, rosemary...optional seasonings include Herbs de Provence (just a little if you want), celery salt (but be careful with salt, the stock usually has enough), marjoram, sage

Sweat the onion and celery along with the garlic &/or shallot if using, as with the mirepoix in chicken & dumplings. Scoop the veg out and brown the meat. If you're using stew meat, I've found I can brown only half the meat and still get the same flavor results from the fond, so that saves time. If you're using ground beef, of course, you need to brown it all. Also, when I make this with stew meat I cut the chunks from the store at least in half; you want smaller chunks than they give you.

Deglaze the pan with the wine (if using) or the stock (if not using wine). Scrape up all that yummy fond, and put the meat and mirepoix back. Add a big spoonful of the tomato paste or half the can of diced tomatoes (with juice), the bay leaf, and the seasonings you've chosen.

If using stew meat, let that simmer about two - two and a half hours, covered. If using ground beef, you can go ahead and add the potato and frozen veg now and simmer about 15 minutes just to meld the flavors a bit.

Add the pearl barley. Cover and simmer 45 min - 1 hour, until the barley is cooked. The barley will thicken the soup, so you might need to add a little more liquid about 2/3 of the way through.

Taste the soup, adjust seasonings. Add the dollop of mustard if using--a Tbsp or two--and stir it well. Cover and simmer a few minutes, taste again.

I sometimes make dumplings for this (my family and I love dumplings). Or I serve it with good buttered bread (or just good bread) or cornbread. Leftovers for this are very versatile; I once stretched a big pot of this an entire week, pouring it over baked potatoes, using it as filling for Yorkshire puddings, as a filling for little pies made of puff pastry...there are lots of possibilities. It only gets better with every day it sits in the fridge because the flavors meld even more.

(Yorkshire puddings:

Equal amounts flour, eggs, and milk. Measure the eggs first--four is usually a good amount and comes to around a cup of egg. Pour the eggs into a large bowl, then measure out the same amount of milk and whisk it into the egg. Add a good pinch of salt. Now measure the same amount of flour and whisk it in. Some Yorkshire pud recipes have you make a well in the flour, but it rises higher if you add the flour to the liquid. Let that mixture sit for at least twenty minutes; you can heat & prep the oven while it does if you're only resting it for 20 min. Preheat oven to 450F. Get out a muffin tin, and into each muffin cup drop a little dollop--maybe a tsp/tsp and a half--of bacon fat/beef drippings/lard/shortening. You MUST use some kind of fat, sorry. Place the muffin tin into the hot oven and let it heat for ten minutes.

At the end of the ten minutes, give the pudding batter another quick whisk. Remove the tin from the oven, and into each cup pour some of the batter--should fill about 1/2 - 3/4, somewhere in between there. (If you're making this with the soup variant--or ou can use seasoned ground beef, or seasoned sausage meat, whatever you like--quickly drop a spoonful of the meat into each cup as well, and put it back into the oven. Let cook about twenty minutes - half an hour, until the puddings have risen very high and are a lovely golden brown and the meat filling is nice and hot. Plain puddings are a lovely side, especially with gravy; when making this with meat filling I serve it with mashed potatoes and gravy.

The basic ingredients of this soup, btw--meat, veg, stock, bay leaf--can be the basis of a number of soups depending on what you like. If you use red wine instead of white, omit the mustard--you can use rice instead of barley, too, if you like, in which case I skip the potato and like to add some soy sauce to it. Or you can add more tomato sauce and add little soup pastas, like orchiette (?) or small macaroni or orzo (which brings me to pasta e fagioli, next). Really, that's all soup is: meat and/or veg simmered in a flavorful liquid. Try the same basic seasonings as this, but with diced pork shoulder and parsnips, with white wine--delicious over rice. You can make my "lazy bourguignonne" by browning a few strips of bacon cut into smaller pieces, removing the bacon (put in fridge to finish soup with), and then browning stew meat with minced onion and garlic in the bacon fat. Make a roux by adding about 1/4 C flour to the pan (might need to melt some butter in there or add a little olive oil) and stirring the flour and fat for a minute or two until well combined. Deglaze the pan with 2 C red wine, add a cup or two of beef stock, and simmer with rosemary, thyme, a couple of bay leaves, and a little parsley. If you have/have access to mushroom ketchup, pour in a glug of that, along with Worcestershire sauce. Simmer for 2 1/2 - 3 hours until meat is tender, then add the bacon back in and cook 15 minutes more. Serve over rice--I make this allll the time (I do a much more elaborate version with cocktail onions and mushrooms for our Christmas dinner ever year, that marinates overnight on Christmas Eve and simmers half the day on Christmas day), it's one of my favorite meals and is so easy. You can also serve with mashed or baked potatoes and some nice crusty bread if you like.

Pasta e Fagioli (This is sort of a combo of Marcella Hazan's recipe and The Olive Garden's, lol. But there's also a good shortcut method, which I'll describe here too):

Mirepoix (which is called a soffritto in Italian cooking)

minced garlic (3-4 cloves)

1-2 lbs ground beef

1/2 lb ground pork (optional. You can also use Italian sausage meat instead if you like a little spice; I don't, but some do)

2 cans beans: cannelini beans OR cranberry beans OR kidney beans OR Great Northern beans, or any combo thereof

2 C beef stock

1 or 2 large can tomato puree or tomato sauce (depends on how much meat you're using)

1 regular-sized can diced tomatoes

seasonings: basil, oregano, a little thyme, dash nutmeg

bay leaf

soup pasta: orzo, small macaroni, dittalini, orchiette, etc. Ditalini is best here.

white wine (optional)

Parmesan cheese, romano cheese (romano optional)

Sweat the soffritto, with the garlic, in olive oil. Remove from pot, and brown the meat (drain the fat if necessary). Add the seasonings (remember, you've already got salt & pepper on the veg there for the sweat). Add the white wine if using, maybe 1/2 C, and the tomato sauce, diced tomatoes, and stock. Pour in both cans of beans with their juice. Give it a good stir. Add a bay leaf and simmer for forty-five minutes - an hour. You want it to reduce a bit but still be, well, soupy, and a little waterier than eating texture because you're going to cook pasta in it, which will soak up a lot of the extra liquid.

Alternatively, instead of using a soffritto and tomatoes etc., you can just brown the meats and add a large jar of whatever purchased or pre-made pasta sauce you like. If using premade sauce, use only 1 C stock and 1 C water. Check for seasonings after it's simmered twenty min or so, and add whatever you think it's missing.

Grate in a good amount of parmesan (or parm & romano), stir it in, simmer a little longer.

About ten minutes before you want to serve, check to make sure the soup is still liquidy enough to cook pasta--if not, add more water, then stir in the pasta (1 box, about one pound) and simmer until cooked.

Serve with more cheese grated on top, if you like, with some good garlic bread or garlic Texas Toast.

I've done both the canned-tomatoes-canned-sauce method and the pre-made-spaghetti-sauce method. They're both good. So it's really up to you. I prefer plain canned puree, but that's because I always make my own tomato sauce for pasta anyway. If you usually use jarred sauce--which is fine of course--or you just don't feel like messing with it, go ahead and use jarred sauce.

...I think that's about it. I make a lot of soups, but they're usually variations of the beef barley--like I said, you can use whatever meats and veg and liquid you like. Once you've made a few soups you'll be able to really start experimenting and having fun with them, finding combos you especially like.

Oh, a good tip to add body to soups/stews: bloom a packet of unflavored gelatin (or soften a sheet of leaf gelatin in cold water, which is my preference) and add the gelatin to the hot soup. Stir it in well. It adds a nice silkiness and body to the soup. You can also use the soup-liquid-and-flour-goo method from the chicken and dumplings recipe to thicken just about any soup, or the roux we made in the beef burguignonne recipe. Keep in mind, too, that any sort of grain added to soup will help thicken it, like the barley or rice or pasta. More than once I've set out to make a beef and rice or chicken and rice soup (which is much like the chicken and dumplings, but add rice about half an hour before serving and let it simmer, and skip the dumplings) and ended up with something more like a burgoo or pilau, but hey, those are also yummy.

Oh, one more! Risi e bisi, rice and pea soup. This is a really nice light soup, and is a traditional spring soup in Italy where it's eaten on April 25 to celebrate Italy's liberation from Nazi & fascist rule):

2 lbs peas, fresh or frozen (frozen is actually better, generally)

3 Tbsp minced onion

2-3 Tbsp butter

2 1/4 C beef stock (the best quality possible; Better than Bouillon is still fine, but if you have homemade or really good store-bought, try it here)

8 oz rice, preferably Italian rice like vialone nano, but any rice will do (except, like, sushi rice)

2 Tbsp chopped parsley

1/4 C or so grated parmesan

Cook the onions in the melted butter on very low heat until the onion is soft and starting to turn golden. Add the peas and a good pinch of salt, and cook about 2 minutes until the peas are thawed (if using frozen) and bright green, and well-coated in the butter.

Pour in all but about 1/4C of the stock; cover and simmer about ten minutes.

Add the rice and the rest of the stock. Cover and simmer about 20-30 minutes, until the rice is cooked (soft but firm, not falling apart).

Stir in the parsley and the grated parm. Taste and correct the salt if needed. Serve with more grated parm on top if desired. Eat while celebrating freedom. :-)
